title: A new algorithm for state-constrained separated continuous linear programs
contribution: Defines state-constrained separated continuous LPs (SCSCLP), a class containing Anderson's SCLP, and gives a successive quadratic programming algorithm that moves breakpoints and controls together, terminates finitely, and yields no duality gap without boundedness assumptions plus piecewise-constant optimal controls, illustrated on reentrant lines with up to 250 continuous variables.
problem_entry: LO+SD: large-scale finite-dimensional and semi-infinite LP had progressed while LP in infinite-dimensional spaces, which models manufacturing and communication systems, had not; Anderson's job-shop SCLP is enlarged by state constraints Fy <= h and a state cost (abstract p. 1; p. 2).
key_idea: Make the discretization breakpoints variables through v = (t_i - t_{i-1}) u, turning the fixed-partition LP DP(P) into a nonconvex QP with polyhedral constraints; compute KKT points (Frank-Wolfe or matrix splitting), purify redundant intervals, double the breakpoints and test global optimality with a dual-related LP discretization AP(P), improving control and partition simultaneously instead of alternating as Pullan does (pp. 8-12, 17-23).
assumptions: Deterministic continuous-time LP with bounded measurable u, y, eta; Assumption 1: a, h continuous, a, c, h piecewise linear, b, g piecewise constant, problem feasible and bounded below; no boundedness of the solution set, with unbounded u and possibly no optimal solution admitted as the key difficulty; bounded solution set and E = I needed for the structure theorem; test data a reentrant line with random service times, costs and initial queues (pp. 1, 4, 9-10, 29, 31).
proof_devices: weak duality by integration by parts with pi(t) of finite variation; complementary slackness characterizes strong duality (Proposition 1, Corollary 1, pp. 4-5)
zero-length intervals carrying mass encode Dirac controls; tau-splitting sequences give V(SCSCLP) <= V(QP(|P|)) for every P (Lemmas 1-2, pp. 9-10)
closed-form interval-merging test, inequality (11), and procedure PURIFY (Lemmas 3-4, Corollary 2, pp. 11-12)
sandwich V(AP(P)) = V(AP*(P)) <= V(SCSCLP*) <= V(SCSCLP) <= V(DP(Q)) by mapping dual-discretization solutions to piecewise-linear dual functions (Theorems 1-2, Corollary 3, pp. 15-17)
doubling of breakpoints and an epsilon-patch with cost change delta + o(epsilon), delta < 0; the first Frank-Wolfe iterate bounds the duality gap (Theorems 3-4, pp. 17-22)

finite termination: injective map from positive-length intervals to generalized extreme points of finitely many linear systems (resolution theorem) plus finitely many KKT values per QP (Luo-Tseng) (Lemmas 5-8, Corollary 4, Theorem 5, pp. 24-29)
strong duality, a piecewise-linear optimal dual and a piecewise-constant optimal control obtained as byproducts of the algorithm (Theorems 6-7, pp. 29-30)
experiments: C on a Sparc 10/41 calling academic LOQO 1.08 for the LP/QP subproblems, with a lower-bound module that builds dual feasible solutions; one random reentrant-line family (Kumar), n stations x 5 classes; Table 9.1 reports objective, pieces, dual objective and time per iteration (primal 5963.6674 vs dual 5963.2700 after 3 iterations, 29 pieces, 2436.61 s); time close to quadratic in 5-25 stations at precision 1e-4, 25 stations = 250 continuous variables; time almost exponential in the accuracy requirement; no baseline algorithm run (pp. 30-32).
positioning: Bellman's CLP and Anderson's SCLP; surveys Lehman, Drews, Hartberger, Segers, Perold and Anstreicher ('still incomplete'), Ilyutovich, Ito-Kelley-Sachs, Anderson-Nash, Pullan (credited as 'the state of the art') and Philpott-Craddock; criticism by restating requirements (Pullan's vanishing mesh and tripled pieces, Anderson-Nash's need for all extreme points); the new dual reduces to Pullan's; cites Avram-Bertsimas-Ricard (pp. 1-2, 4, 18, 24).
writing: Abstract opens with a field contrast and lists six claims; contribution paragraph, roadmap and a reading instruction ('first read sections 2 and 6'); informal argument before the convergence proof; theorem-dense; 'efficient' and 'several hundred continuous variables' in the abstract versus growth almost exponential in accuracy and 250 variables in the body (Tension T6); closing 'We believe' (pp. 1-3, 23, 31-32).
limits_future: Stated: exact solution far harder than approximation (time almost exponential in accuracy), piecewise-linear/constant data only, bounded solution set and E = I for the structure result; not stated [card-writer's reading]: no rate or complexity bound, one random instance family, no comparison with Pullan or Philpott-Craddock; future: exploit the structure of the intermediate QPs (pp. 4, 29, 32).

method_links.note: An infinite-dimensional LP owned by optimal control is rewritten as a sequence of finite QPs solved by an off-the-shelf solver, and the dual is read for certificates and structure; but the reformulation leaves LP for a nonconvex QP and relies on an LP-dual optimality test instead of a class-keeping device; solve times are measured at the application scale.
Certificate part only: the algorithm stops on a primal-dual gap and every reported iteration carries its dual bound; no incumbent duel.
Weak: the journal version of a student's thesis problem class (Luo 1995), funded by a PYI award with Draper Laboratory matching funds.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: duality as the byproduct of an algorithm
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Strong duality without boundedness and the structure of optimal solutions are proved through the finite termination of Algorithm A, even when no optimal solution exists.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-derive classical theorems with the new device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The duality and piecewise-constant-structure results of the SCLP literature are recovered and extended as consequences of the algorithm (also S121, S007).

transferable: [D1] Enlarge a studied class by the constraint type the application needs and show that the old class is a special case (pp. 2, 4).
[D2] Turn an unknown discretization into decision variables via v = dt*u; settle for KKT points of the resulting nonconvex QP and certify global optimality with a dual discretization (pp. 8-10, 17).
[D2] Merge intervals whenever a closed-form test shows the merge lowers the cost, so convergence does not depend on mesh refinement (pp. 10-12, 24).
[D4] Represent Dirac controls as zero-length intervals carrying mass and approximate them by tau-splitting sequences instead of excluding them by assumption (pp. 9-10).
[D4] Bound the number of pieces by an injective map to extreme points of finitely many linear systems (pp. 24-29).
[D5] Report primal value, dual bound, model size and time per iteration in one table (p. 32).

quotes.text: We prove algorithmically the absence of a duality gap for this class of problems without any boundedness assumptions on the solution set.
It is our experience that (SCSCLP) is easier to approximate than to solve exactly.

title: Portfolio construction through mixed-integer programming at Grantham, Mayo, Van Otterloo and Company
contribution: Describes GMO's deployment of a mixed-integer program that tracks QP-built target portfolios (single and multi-subportfolio) with far fewer names and trading tickets under piecewise-linear liquidity and transaction costs, used for 11 portfolios worth $8.158 billion with average reductions of 48.7% in names and 79.3% in tickets and about $4 million a year saved.
problem_entry: IO+AP: a practice complication outside Markowitz QP theory (many names and tickets raise costs) became a business crisis at GMO (1,000-1,500 securities against a norm near 200, clients threatening to leave); thresholding small positions was rejected in the owner's terms (small-cap strategy, loss of control); MIP was chosen because the counts are integer (pp. 2, 4-6).
key_idea: Replace the QP target plus thresholding by one MIP with seven penalized terms (L1 distance to target, sector deviation, names and tickets indicators, minus expected return, convex piecewise-linear illiquidity and transaction costs), optimizing subportfolios jointly so that they cross trades; one model runs in tracking or performance-enhancing mode (pp. 6-8, 10, 13).
assumptions: Linear MIP with binaries for names and tickets; data are GMO's current and target weights, multifactor return forecasts, sector memberships, illiquidity and volume indices; risk enters only through the QP-built target; monthly rebalancing; penalties chosen heuristically through thousands of 20-year historical simulations (pp. 3, 6-9, 17-18).
proof_devices: absolute values linearized by paired inequalities; convex piecewise-linear costs modelled by bounded segment variables without binaries (pp. 7-8, 17)
big-M link w_f(i) <= y_names(i) strengthened to w_f(i) <= a_i w_max y_names(i) with market-cap-dependent constants for a stronger relaxation (pp. 17-18)
branching priorities and directions from the target solution: largest target positions first, keep-first for large and eliminate-first for small positions (p. 10)
CPLEX stopping criterion and allowed suboptimality tuned; no theorems (p. 10)
experiments: FORTRAN 90 (about 10,000 lines) around CPLEX 4.0 on a DEC AlphaServer 4100 5/466; 15 CPU hours per 1,500-security problem in October 1996 cut to a few minutes (Table 1: up to 6,546 x 51,532, 0.4-4.0 CPU minutes); UK backtest 1977-1997 in tracking mode (80/146 names, 60% fewer tickets), US small-growth backtest 1982-1997 in performance-enhancing mode (2.0x vs 1.6x the benchmark, 55% fewer names, 80% fewer tickets); live: 11 portfolios, $8.158 billion, average 48.7% fewer names and 79.3% fewer tickets; baselines are the owner's target portfolio and the benchmark index; no gaps reported; penalties tuned on the same history used for evaluation [card-writer's reading] (pp. 8-16).
positioning: Cites only Markowitz (1959); claims no known MIP use in portfolio practice and no prior academic description of the problem, and that multi-subportfolio optimization has not been addressed by others (pp. 2, 4, 18).
writing: Interfaces genre: firm and crisis first, then model, implementation, results and impact; six numbered benefits in the abstract; pull quotes; the founder's testimonial; hedged ('and we expect that it will') and promotional ('This free lunch'); 'globally optimize' up front while suboptimality tolerances were tuned (Tension T6) (pp. 1-6, 10, 16-18).
limits_future: Stated: return gains seen only in simulation, no variable-cost savings from fewer positions, execution-cost reduction difficult to quantify; not stated [card-writer's reading]: no gaps or tolerances reported, no hold-out period for penalty tuning, Table 2 market values headed $ billion but in $ million; future: the large-stock US funds and goals beyond tracking (pp. 8, 10, 13, 16-17).

method_links.note: Owner, decision, data and current rule (QP target plus thresholding, rejected in the owner's terms); decision metrics (names, tickets, turnover, return relative to the benchmark); backtest before live deployment; one applied paper per deployment; own run times reported, including the initial 15 hours.

The model stays a linear MIP (linearized absolute values and convex costs) solved by a commercial solver at the application scale with measured times; the formulation was strengthened to improve LP bounds, a 1999 data point for Tension T4.

Step 1 holds (one joint MIP replaces greedy postprocessing), but the incumbent is rejected by argument rather than dueled, and no certificate or gap is reported while the allowed suboptimality was tuned (Tension T1).
Seven penalties set heuristically by thousands of simulation runs, not one interpretable knob with a published price curve (pre-2004).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: historical back-simulation as the adoption gate
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Two decades of the owner's own history simulated to convince top management before deployment; live results reported separately.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: structure-informed branching from the target solution
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Branch first on the largest target positions; keep-first for large positions, eliminate-first for small ones.

transferable: [D1] State the business objection to the owner's current shortcut before proposing the exact model (p. 5).
[D2] Run one model in two modes for two owner goals (tracking vs performance-enhancing) by changing only the penalties (pp. 10, 13).
[D4] Model convex piecewise-linear costs with bounded segment variables and keep binaries for the counts only (pp. 7-8, 17).
[D4] Strengthen big-M links with problem-specific caps (pp. 17-18).
[D4] Set branching priorities and directions from the structure of the target solution (p. 10).
[D5] Keep simulated results (backtests) and implemented results (live portfolios) in separate sections and tables, and report the solve-time history with the changes that produced it (pp. 9-16).

quotes.text: Since the number of positions and trades in the composite portfolio is an inherently integer quantity, we decided that we would use mixed-integer-programming methods to globally optimize the portfolio.
Prior to implementing the mixed-integer-programming approach, we performed extensive historical simulations. We used these to convince top management at GMO of the effectiveness of the method.

title: On dependent randomized rounding algorithms
contribution: Introduces dependent randomized rounding (one shared uniform threshold, with mirrored, sequential, comb and split variants) that gives direct integrality proofs for s-t cut, sign-balanced Boolean optimization, uncapacitated lot-sizing and k-median on a cycle, a 2-approximation for feasible cut, and a tight 2(1 - 1/2^k) bound for min-k-sat (3/2 for min-2-sat).
problem_entry: IO: randomized rounding rounded variables independently and used few structural results of the fractional optimum (Raghavan-Thompson, Goemans-Williamson, Bertsimas-Vohra); Grotschel-Lovasz note that rounding 'appropriately' is not sufficiently analyzed; target: variants of the min-cut type (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Correlate the rounding through one random number: a single threshold U, U and 1 - U across a bipartition, sequential thresholds, a comb {U, 1+U, ..., k-1+U} over intervals of length y_j, U restricted to [1/2, 1], or a random A/B split, so that expected rounded values reproduce the LP's own terms and the analysis becomes simple (pp. 2-9).
assumptions: 0-1 IPs with nonnegative costs and their LP relaxations, undirected graphs unless stated; lot-sizing without backlogging and with zero lead time, a cost condition proved only in a special case, and an LP augmented by valid ordering inequalities; min-k-sat with at most k literals per clause after preprocessing; no data (pp. 2, 5, 9).
proof_devices: integrality sandwich Z_LP <= Z_IP <= E(Z_H) = Z_LP with E[edge cut] = P(min <= U <= max) = |y(u) - y(v)| (Theorem 1, p. 3)
max-flow-min-cut theorem via LP duality for directed cuts; threshold rounding preserves precedence constraints (p. 3)
U and 1 - U across a sign-balanced bipartition reproduce min(x_i, x_j) and max(0, x_i + x_j - 1) (Theorem 2, p. 4)
exchange argument adds valid ordering inequalities; induction gives P(y_i = 1) = y_i (Theorem 3, pp. 5-6)
systematic sampling over consecutive intervals on a cycle (Theorem 4, pp. 6-7)
case analysis with U in [1/2, 1] gives factor 2 for feasible cut (Theorem 5, p. 8)
union bound plus a favourable-split probability 2/2^k gives 2(1 - 1/2^k) for min-k-sat (Theorem 6, p. 9)
tight example with all 2^k sign patterns: Z_IP = 2(1 - 1/2^k) Z_LP (pp. 9-10)
positioning: Credits Raghavan-Thompson, Goemans-Williamson, Bertsimas-Vohra, Bronnimann-Goodrich and deterministic-rounding work; matches Yu-Cheriyan and Ravi for feasible cut; improves Kohli et al. for min-2-sat (2 to 3/2); concedes that Linial-London-Rabinovich give the same s-t cut proof (pointed out by a referee) and that Hochbaum's half-integrality refines the factor-2 results (pp. 1-3, 7).
writing: Short letter; a quoted survey sentence motivates the gap; the generic two-step template, then 'The heart of the rounding procedure ... is in the design of the randomization scheme'; contribution framed as simplicity of analysis; explicit scoping sentence; one geometry figure; ends on a tightness example; referee thanked for discrepancies in an earlier version (pp. 1-3, 9-10).
limits_future: Stated: no running-time analysis or derandomization, lot-sizing proof for a special case, factor-2 results subsumed by half-integrality, scope limited to min-cut-type variants; no future work stated (pp. 2, 5, 7).

method_links.note: Domain Map IO row (LP-relaxation rounding): the LP relaxation is the engine, integrality and approximation are read off the LP solution by rounding, LP duality ties the directed cut to max-flow, and the boundary is printed as the integrality gap through a tight example.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: probabilistic reading of a relaxation solution
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: LP values treated as marginal probabilities and the rounding correlated so that expectations reproduce the LP's terms (S007 has the SDP covariance version).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-derive classical theorems with the new device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Integrality of classical polyhedra (s-t cut, lot-sizing, k-median on a cycle) and the max-flow-min-cut theorem recovered by one rounding argument (also S156, S007).

transferable: [D2] Couple the rounding through one shared random threshold (or U and 1 - U across a bipartition) so that joint probabilities equal the LP's min/max terms (pp. 3-4).
[D4] Prove integrality by the sandwich Z_LP <= Z_IP <= E(Z_H) = Z_LP (p. 3).
[D4] Before rounding, add valid inequalities that an exchange argument shows some optimal LP solution satisfies, to give it the monotone structure the rounding needs (p. 5).
[D4] Close an approximation result with an instance whose IP/LP ratio equals the bound, showing the analysis is tight for that relaxation (pp. 9-10).
[D7] Frame a technique paper by the simplicity of its analysis and state plainly what is not covered (running time, derandomization) (p. 2).

quotes.text: Few structural results of the fractional optimum solution have been used in the design of the rounding heuristics.
The key advantage of this approach is that by using dependencies in the rounding process, the analysis of the performance of the rounding heuristic becomes extremely simple.

title: Moment problems and semidefinite optimization
contribution: Surveys how convex and semidefinite optimization answer moment problems in four fields (tight multivariate Markov and Chebyshev bounds with NP-hardness boundaries, option-price bounds from moments with a polynomial-time separation algorithm, SDP relaxations of queueing-network achievable regions, covariance-based rounding of SDP relaxations), adding computations in which SDP lower bounds improve the LP relaxation by 55-60% and come close to fluid-derived heuristic policies.
problem_entry: CP+SD+AP+IO: one question list per field: are Markov, Chebyshev and Chernoff best possible and generalizable; model-free option-price bounds from moments; lower bounds for EXPTIME-hard queueing-network scheduling using the fact that performance vectors are moments; a general way to round SDP relaxations (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: The feasible moment sequence is the key connection: moment feasibility is a PSD condition, so (i) PSD constraints strengthen achievable-region LPs, (ii) tight bounds are LPs over measures whose duals are polynomial-domination problems solved through separation, (iii) option bounds are sup E[phi(X)] under moment constraints, (iv) an SDP solution is read as a covariance matrix for sampling and rounding (pp. 4-6, 9, 15, 21-23, 27-29, 33-34).
assumptions: Moment information (n, k, Omega); strong duality needs an interior moment vector (boundary handled by restricting the support); full-rank covariance assumed without loss of generality; a membership oracle for S; open multiclass queueing network with Poisson arrivals, exponential service, Markovian routing, steady state and preemptive nonidling policies, lower bounds only; finance: no-arbitrage only and a zero interest rate (pp. 7-8, 21-24, 26-27).
proof_devices: PSD characterization of feasible moment sequences: Hankel matrices (Theorem 1, pp. 4-5) and [[1, M'], [M, Gamma]] PSD via the covariance argument and a normal construction (Theorem 2, pp. 5-6)

lift-and-project relaxation of the achievable region: projection, definitional and lower-bound identities, flow conservation L- = L+ on aggregated S-queues by a sample-path argument, and PSD constraints (Theorems 3-6, pp. 9-15)

LP duality over measures: weak duality from chi_S <= g, strong duality and complementary slackness (Isii, Smith) with discrete extremal distributions; optimization equivalent to separation (Theorems 7-8, pp. 22-23, 29)
tight bounds as convex programs: multivariate Markov (Theorem 9, p. 23) and multivariate Chebyshev 1/(1 + d^2) with d the Mahalanobis distance from the mean to S (Theorem 10, pp. 24-25)
NP-hardness by co-positivity for (n,2,R+^n) and by a 3SAT reduction for (n,k,R^n); the OCR file reads 'k > 3', so the threshold (k >= 3 or k >= 4) is not settled by this text (p. 26)
polynomial-time separation: PSD test of A-bar = sum y_i A_i - A with a negative-eigenvector witness, then convex QPs (Theorem 11, Algorithms A-B, pp. 29-31)
dual tangency argument re-proving Lo's tight call-price bound (Theorem 12, pp. 31-32)
covariance rounding x = sign(X), X ~ N(0, Y); Sheppard's arcsin formula and the Goemans-Williamson inequality give 0.878 (Proposition 1, Theorem 13, pp. 33-35)
experiments: Two queueing examples, LP vs SDP relaxation vs a simulated fluid-derived heuristic policy: a two-station network with arrival rate 0.1-1.18 (SDP 283 variables, 259 constraints, SDPA, under 1 minute on a Pentium II, LBFS-B threshold chosen by simulation) and a four-class single station (SDP 234 x 220, under 2 minutes); the SDP improves the LP by 55-60% (more at high traffic) and is close to the policy, and in the second case improves the LP often by an order of magnitude; solver accuracy failures reported with primal and dual feasible values; table values unreadable in the OCR file (pp. 16-19).
positioning: Credits the classical moment problem (Karlin-Shapley, Akhiezer, Kemperman), Isii and Smith (Smith's procedure criticized as far from an actual algorithm), Lo, Cox-Ross, Harrison-Kreps, Goemans-Williamson, Papadimitriou-Tsitsiklis and Lovasz-Schrijver; a third of the 30 references are the group's own, including S156 and Bertsimas-Ye (pp. 4, 9, 14, 20, 26, 31, 33, 36-38).
writing: Question lists per field and an abstract made of questions; a one-sentence central message; a recurring register of surprise ('often unexpected', 'Surprisingly', 'unexpected improvements'); historical depth for effect (results known in 1900); attributed hedges ('perhaps the most promising methodology', 'we believe'); a short two-item closing; several results stated without proof (pp. 1-4, 18, 23-26, 34-35).
limits_future: Stated: complexity of higher-order moment feasibility unresolved, lower bounds only, SDP solver accuracy problems, NP-hardness beyond second moments or on the nonnegative orthant, 0.878 not known to be tight; future: fluid-control policies combined with SDP bounds, SDP for better lower bounds in stochastic optimization, non-normal rounding distributions (pp. 6, 8, 16, 18, 26, 35).

method_links.note: Probability, finance and queueing problems written as convex/SDP programs; the dual gives worst-case distributions; the tractability boundary is printed; the questions recorded as SW2's origin already frame this 2000 chapter; a [stated-joint] CP methodology claim (convex optimization as the natural way; optimization leads to unexpected improvements of classical results).
Certificate part in SD: the SDP relaxation is valued for its suboptimality guarantees on heuristic policies, and primal and dual feasible values are reported when the solver fails.
Weak: a chapter written with two students packaging one programme's results across four fields.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: probabilistic reading of a relaxation solution
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The SDP matrix is read as a covariance matrix, sampled from N(0, Y) and rounded by sign (also S121).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-derive classical theorems with the new device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Markov and Chebyshev generalized, the scalar one-sided Chebyshev bound improved, Lo's bound and the 0.878 max-cut bound re-proved (also S121, S156).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: policy from one model, bound from another
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Fluid-control policies (Luo-Bertsimas, S156) certified by SDP lower bounds, proposed as the most promising methodology for multiclass queueing networks.

transferable: [D1] Open a survey with one list of concrete questions per field in which the common object appears (pp. 2-3).
[D2] Turn the fact that the variables are moments into a PSD constraint and add it to any relaxation whose variables are expectations (pp. 5-6, 15).
[D4] Derive linear constraints on performance moments from a conservation law applied to every aggregate S-queue (pp. 12-14).
[D4] For tight probability bounds, dualize the LP over measures into a polynomial-domination problem and solve it through separation (pp. 21-23, 29-31).
[D4] Prove a separation problem polynomial by a PSD test with a negative-eigenvector witness, followed by convex QPs (pp. 29-30).
[D5] Compare relaxations against a simulated heuristic policy, not only against each other (pp. 17-18).
coauthors: Ioana Popescu, Jay Sethuraman (title page of the April 2000 manuscript; the work list gives J Sethuraman only)

quotes.text: Optimization not only offers a natural way to formulate and study such problems, it leads to unexpected improvements of classical results.

Both computational experiments demonstrate that, unlike the LP relaxation, the semidefinite relaxation provides practically useful suboptimality guarantees that can be used to assess the closeness to optimality of heuristic policies.
